Councillor Davey Thank you and good afternoon everyone. This will take a bit of time because
we are going through the issues of the budget so a bit of a document to read for me. So
As Chair of Finance and Corporate Services Committee, it is my pleasure to table the
2025 budget on behalf of Mayor Vrbanovic.
As Council is aware, for the public's benefit, I think it's important to provide some background
on why since 2024 the City's budget is now referred to as the Mayor's proposed budget.
On July 1, 2023, the province amended legislation to provide strong mayor powers to select municipalities
in Ontario, including Kitchener.
As part of that change, current legislation now requires that the Mayor be the one to
propose the Municipal Budget for the upcoming year.
This change required the City to adapt to a slightly different budget process last year,
and we have once again followed a similar process to this year's budget.
When proposing the budget, both the Mayor and myself as Chair have endeavoured to do
so in a manner consistent with the collaborative approach that has existed between Kitchener
Council and staff in our work over many years. Based on the direction that was
provided earlier this year, City staff provided a draft budget informed by
Council and community priorities in alignment with the City's approved
financial guidelines and policies. The draft 2025 budget was presented to
Council for consideration and discussion at Budget Committee meetings held on
November 18th and again on the 25th. The 2025 draft budget that was prepared by
staff and presented for Council's consideration builds on the success of
previous budgets by continuing to address the priorities that are important for Kitchener and
its residents. From delivering the programs and services that residents and business rely on
every day, to investments in infrastructure that help address the city's asset replacement and
growth related needs, to providing funding to implement the city's 2023 to 2026 strategic plan
that will help shape Kitchener's future. The 2025 draft budget balances several priorities and
continues the trend of delivering good value for Kitchener residents.
In developing this proposed budget, Kitchener City Council and staff acknowledged the challenging
economic environment that residents have faced over recent years and we have endeavored to
do our part to keep property taxes as low as possible without sacrificing service-related
needs.
A proposed tax increase of 3.9% as outlined in the budget maintains existing service levels
for the approximately 50 core services the City provides and still responds to growth-related
pressures that come with welcoming new residents to Kitchener each year.
It also ensures that Kitchener's average property tax increase over the 10 years remains below
Ontario's inflation rate increases during that same time period.
Kitchener has continued to grow over the past many years and is now home to over 300,000
residents.
Even with the increased pressure of serving a larger population base, the City has been
able to keep pace, carefully balancing increasing service needs while still proposing budget
increases that we believe are reasonable.
Kitchener's tax levy per capita is one of the lowest in the province when compared to
other large municipalities in Ontario.
It also has what's considered a low municipal burden, which combines both taxes and utility
rates when comparing Kitchener to other municipalities.
Although Kitchener only makes up 30% of the residential tax bill and the region representing
57% with the education taxes making up the remaining 13, Kitchener has always
demonstrated his commitment to considering affordability when setting
its budget, consistently delivering tax rate increases that are aligned with the
rate of inflation in Ontario. Kitchener's track record speaks for
itself when it comes to balancing affordability, service demands and
responding to growth related pressures. I am proud of Council and staff's
approach to rate setting and believe Kitchener is a model of efficient,
effective and sustainable local government in Ontario.
During the past 10 years, Kitchener's tax rate increases have averaged 2.47%, below
Ontario inflation which has averaged 2.64% during the same time frame.
This should give residents confidence that they are getting good value for the programs
and services that the City provides.
Kitchener is also making important investments in infrastructure, recognizing the need to
take care of the $10 billion worth of assets the City is responsible for, while also moving
forward with new infrastructure that's needed to support housing and a growing community.
The City's 1.9 billion capital budget identifies the infrastructure that is planned to be replaced
over the next 10 years.
Although the City's planned investment over 10 years is significant, it's important to
reiterate that this is still not enough to address all of the City's infrastructure
replacement needs, and we join in calls for a new fiscal arrangement for municipalities
over the long term with both the provincial and federal orders of government to address
this gap.
Despite these challenges, the City has been proactive in trying to address infrastructure
funding needs, including launching the Water Infrastructure Program, as we all know as
WIPP, in 2017 to fund replacement of underground infrastructure.
By moving to a more predictable rate model, the City has been able to fund approximately
$400 million in capital infrastructure replacement since the program was established, and we
are currently in the second year of that Council-approved WIPP program.
Additional funding for the rehabilitation of aging facility infrastructure has been increasing
by approximately $5 million per year since 2019, and facilities continue to be a significant
funding priority within the capital budget, with an additional $6 million added in funding
Allocating $1.4 million in 2025 to the City's Energy Retrofit Reserve to replace components
and facilities with smart, energy-efficient solutions is helping to move the City towards
a more sustainable, low-carbon future while also providing operational savings over time.
I just pause here for a second to note that we have been accomplishing all of this despite
not introducing an infrastructure tax levy which other municipalities have done which
simply adds in addition to the tax levy it increases each year.
Besides the City's own efforts and strategies to try and address the capital funding needs,
staff have also pursued federal and provincial grant opportunities, successfully securing
over $200 million in federal and provincial funding over the past five years.
It's important for the City to continue to be proactive in this space, ensuring that
funding opportunities are fully explored, including continuing with advocacy efforts
for additional infrastructure funding, since this represents the most significant funding
challenge that municipalities face moving forward.
In addition to the rehabilitation of existing infrastructure, the City also needs to provide
new infrastructure to support a growing community.
This infrastructure is funded through development charges and not through property taxes, maintaining
the concept that growth should pay for growth.
As the city continues to expand, particularly in the southwest area of the city, new amenities
are needed to support the recreational needs.
This includes $16 million for the construction of a new library branch in southwest Kitchener
that will be fully operational in 2025, $6 million for the Rosenberg Community Centre
that will provide programming and space for the surrounding neighbourhood, and last but
not least, certainly the $144 million for the Kitchener Indoor Recreation Facility that
will be located in Schlegel Park and will include an indoor pool, FIFA-sized local soccer facility,
and provide other important gathering spaces for residents in the community. Finally, the city is
in the second year of implementing its 2023-2026 strategic plan. The 2025 budget continues to build
on investments made through last year's budget process, with funding allocated within budget to
support actions identified under the five goal areas within the strategic plan, including building
a connected city together, cultivating a green city together, creating an economic and economically
thriving city together, fostering a caring city together, and stewarding a best city together.
The 2025 budget highlights approximately 75 million dollars in funding that will help
to advance strategic priorities. This includes 56 million in federal and provincial funding
the city has received to advance the affordable housing initiatives. Some of the investments
and other important areas include $8.6 million towards advancing actions in the City Parks Master Plan,
including improvements being made at Upper Canada Park and McLennan Park,
$1.3 million towards the implementation of the City's Tree Canopy Plan,
and $800,000 in green fleet improvements, including the replacement of three ice resurfacing machines to electric,
$780,000 in operating and capital funding to support the activation of the Conrad Centre,
and $100,000 to increase spots in summer camps for youth.
These examples and more build on progress made
in the previous year, helping the city deliver
on key priorities and commitments,
including the 2023-2026 strategic plan.
In addition to these investments,

and proposed.

with the following strategic investment related to additional $1 million in one-time capital
funding.

This investment will see the installation of new courts in underserviced areas of the
city or enhance the condition of existing courts.

for residents of all ages in neighbourhoods across Kitchener.
In closing, the City's 20-year vision included in the City's 2023-2026 strategic plan is
building a city for everyone where together we take care of the world around us and each
other.
